article_title: NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts
citation: Mohammed I. Radaideh, Jeremy Moon, Andre Gala-Garza, Emma Son, Yug Shah, Majdi I. Radaideh. (2026). NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts. Preprint submitted to Peer Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04030
title: Curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images with automated extraction pipeline and released SDXL checkpoint
description: A curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images assembled from three sources: 348 images from books and encyclopedias, 119 from journal publications, and 533 from nuclear news websites. Images were extracted via a three-stage Python pipeline (CLIP-ViT-L/14 zero-shot classification, then GPT-4.1-nano and GPT-5-nano filtering) and preprocessed by upscaling to 1024x1024 with GPT-Image-2 while removing text and arrows. The article states the dataset "provides a foundation for future research in domain-specific generative AI". The best SDXL checkpoint and 300 testing prompts are released on GitHub.
requirements: Images require captions and preprocessing (upscaling, text and arrow removal) because the SD and Flux.1 models could not generate readable text even after fine-tuning
constraints: The article notes nuclear engineering has limited publicly accessible high-quality annotated images, so large-scale dataset expansion is challenging; captions from sources may be short and not sufficiently descriptive
target_learners: engineering students and learners of nuclear energy concepts
target_learning_goals: generating technically accurate visual representations of nuclear energy concepts such as reactors, fuel assemblies, fuel cycles, and radiation
examples: The pipeline reduced 41,342 extracted captioned images from 11,600 PDFs to 13,453 (GPT-4.1-nano), then 3,441 (GPT-5-nano), then 119 after manual inspection
key_sources: Mohammed I. Radaideh, Jeremy Moon, Andre Gala-Garza, Emma Son, Yug Shah, Majdi I. Radaideh. (2026). NuclearDiffusion: Text-to-Image Foundation Models for Learning Nuclear Energy Concepts. Preprint submitted to Peer Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04030

article_title: Kindergartners’ fluent processing of symbolic numerical magnitude is predicted by their cardinal knowledge and implicit understanding of arithmetic 2 years earlier
citation: Moore, A. M., vanMarle, K., & Geary, D. C. (2016). Kindergartners' Fluent Processing of Symbolic Numerical Magnitude is Predicted by Their Cardinal Knowledge and Implicit Understanding of Arithmetic Two Years Earlier. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2016.05.003
title: Number sets test as a measure of fluent magnitude processing predicting later mathematics outcomes
description: The number sets test asks children to quickly circle domino-like combinations of objects, Arabic numerals, or both that sum to a target value, with a 60-second limit and signal-detection (d-prime) scoring. The article reports that first-grade performance "correctly identified 2 out of 3 children who were diagnosed with MLD several years later and 9 out of 10 children who received no such diagnosis", with sensitivity and specificity better than first-grade achievement scores and no prediction of reading achievement. In this study it served as the kindergarten outcome measuring fluent processing of symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitudes.
requirements: Requires children to combine nonsymbolic or symbolic magnitudes to match a target numeral under speeded conditions
constraints: Does not capture the full breadth of symbolic number-system knowledge, only fluent processing and manipulation of quantities associated with Arabic numerals
target_learners: preschool and kindergarten children
elementary students at risk of mathematical learning disability
target_learning_goals: fluent processing and manipulation of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical magnitudes
examples: Used as the kindergarten outcome in this study, scored with d-prime (hits minus false alarms) with Cronbach's alphas from .70 to .90
key_sources: Moore, A. M., vanMarle, K., & Geary, D. C. (2016). Kindergartners' Fluent Processing of Symbolic Numerical Magnitude is Predicted by Their Cardinal Knowledge and Implicit Understanding of Arithmetic Two Years Earlier. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2016.05.003

article_title: Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children With Mathematical Learning Disability
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046
title: Number Sets Test d-prime measure of fluent processing of small numerosities and Arabic numerals
description: The Number Sets Test, developed by Geary et al. (2007), assesses the speed and accuracy with which children match combinations of object sets and Arabic numerals to target sums of 5 or 9 within time limits (60 s and 90 s per page). A receiver operating characteristic analysis yields a d-prime sensitivity score controlling for response bias. The article reports that "The d-prime scores, but not response bias scores, are correlated with mathematics but not reading achievement, above and beyond the influence of IQ, working memory, and prior grade mathematics and reading achievement scores," and that first-grade d-prime predicted third-grade MLD status better than first-grade mathematics achievement scores.
requirements: Administration with printed time limits (60 sec per page for target 5; 90 sec for target 9) to avoid ceiling effects and assess fluency
ROC analysis to derive the d-prime sensitivity score controlling for response bias
constraints: Items involve magnitudes within and just beyond the subitizing range (< 10)
target_learners: elementary school children in first through fourth grade
target_learning_goals: fluent processing and manipulation of small exact numerosities and Arabic numerals
examples: In the current study the d-prime intercept was one of four mathematical cognition variables entered into the covariate-adjusted group comparison
key_sources: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046

article_title: Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development
citation: Negen, J., & Sarnecka, B. W. (2012). Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01815.x
title: Number-knower-level framework: children learn one, two, three (and sometimes four) one at a time, then make an inductive leap to the cardinality principle.
description: The framework describes stages of number-word knowledge: children first recite a count list that is "largely empty of meaning", then learn meanings of "one," "two," "three" (and sometimes "four") one at a time and in order, being called one-knowers, two-knowers, and so on. Sometime after learning these, children make a "major inductive leap" understanding that the last word counted indicates the cardinality of the set — the cardinality principle — becoming CP-knowers. The article uses Give-N task performance to assign each child a knower-level, which serves as the dependent measure throughout.
requirements: Give-N task data with titration-style adaptive trials to classify each child's knower-level
constraints: Knower-level coding as zero through five, spaced evenly, yields correlations smaller than effect-size measures allowing unequal group distances
target_learners: typically-developing children aged 30–60 months
target_learning_goals: acquisition of exact cardinal number-word meanings
examples: Experiment 1's Give-N yielded 3 pre-number-knowers, 4 one-knowers, 4 two-knowers, 2 three-knowers, 2 four-knowers, and 11 CP-knowers
key_sources: Negen, J., & Sarnecka, B. W. (2012). Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01815.x

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Design learning environments around an optimal knowledge gap, valued information, and curiosity-reinforcing feedback
description: The review translates its curiosity account into design guidance: "The first step to instigate curiosity is creating an optimal knowledge gap and helping students to be aware of it," for example by introducing cognitive incongruity after basic knowledge, posing provocative questions, or withholding critical information. Teachers should also raise the perceived value and lower the perceived cost of information seeking, and use prompt informative feedback so students learn to enjoy being curious.
requirements: Learners must be aware of the information gap for curiosity to spark
constraints: Outcome-oriented assessment and normative evaluation can undermine curiosity by promoting anxiety about competence
target_learners: K-12 students in teacher-led classrooms
target_learning_goals: Curiosity initiation, maintenance, and deep cognitive exploration
examples: The review recommends introducing an exception that deviates from previously learned knowledge, ill-defined problems or problem-based learning, and personalizing material to increase relevance
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: The contributions of domain-general and numerical factors to third-grade arithmetic skills and mathematical learning disability.
citation: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097
title: Number line estimation task (0-1000)
description: A numerical estimation measure in which children estimated the position of 22 numbers on a scale from 0-1,000, using a different 25 cm number line for each estimate. Estimates were converted into numerical values and mean percent absolute errors were calculated as in Booth and Siegler (2006). This measure served as the estimation factor in the study's regression models and was one of the two multidigit skills assessed.
requirements: Individual number lines for each estimate; target numbers presented in fixed order
target_learners: Third-grade children
target_learning_goals: Numerical magnitude estimation
key_sources: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097

article_title: The contributions of domain-general and numerical factors to third-grade arithmetic skills and mathematical learning disability.
citation: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097
title: Number system knowledge test (32 items)
description: A multidigit skills measure comprising 32 items assessing number naming (e.g., "What number comes five numbers after 49?"), relative magnitude (e.g., "Which is more? 69 or 71?"), numerical distance, oral number sequence recitation (e.g., from 194 to 210), and written number sequence continuation (e.g., from 899 to 901). Items were derived from the Number Knowledge Test (Griffin, 1997) plus additional sequence items. This measure was the second multidigit skill factor in the regression models.
requirements: Oral and written administration covering numbers well above 100
target_learners: Third-grade children
target_learning_goals: Number system knowledge including place value and sequence generation
examples: Written sequence items required children to continue sequences such as from 70,001 to 69,999
key_sources: Cowan, R., & Powell, D. (2014). The Contributions of Domain-General and Numerical Factors to Third-Grade Arithmetic Skills and Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(1), 214-229. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034097

article_title: Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"?
citation: Winch, W. H. (1910). Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Seek numerical accuracy in school arithmetic for its practical value in life, not on the expectation that it will transfer to arithmetical reasoning
description: This pedagogical principle holds that drill aimed at numerical computation should be justified by computation's own usefulness rather than by expected gains in reasoning. Winch concludes that teachers may in some cases improve one function by improving another, but for arithmetic "numerical accuracy should be sought for because it is valuable in actual life, and not because we can feel confident that an improvement in it will transfer to accuracy of arithmetical reasoning". The principle is pending more conclusive experiments.
requirements: The article states indirect improvement of a function should only be attempted if the indirect method is quantitatively better than the direct one, or the direct method is not available.
constraints: The author hedges the conclusion pending more conclusive experiments, and the experimental results across the four schools were too irregular to warrant a conclusion of definite transfer.
target_learners: Elementary school children in Standards II-VII studying arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Accuracy in numerical computation
Accuracy in arithmetical reasoning
examples: In the four experiments, one matched half of each class practised rule sums while the other did history, drawing, geography or English composition, and both were retested on problems marked for reasoning only.
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1910). Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072557

article_title: Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain
citation: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9
title: Number-fact retrieval task with eight arbitrary numeric facts
description: An online task (built with PsychoJs, run on Pavlovia) in which participants learn the results of 8 novel numeric facts presented with the nonexistent operator '&' (e.g., "3&8 = 29"), using only single-digit operands and 2-digit results with digits 2–9. Performance is quantified by a recall score where a correct result digit in the correct position scored 1 point and each correct digit in the incorrect position scored 0.5, scaled 0–100, plus response times and forced-choice tests with confidence ratings. It was used to mimic numeric fact learning in adults already familiar with elementary arithmetic.
requirements: Participants already familiar with elementary arithmetic; facts generated with low between-fact similarity to avoid disrupting learning
constraints: The facts are arbitrary with no systematic rule, so the task isolates rote memorization rather than conceptual or rule-based arithmetic learning
target_learners: Adults (ages 20-40) familiar with elementary arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Memorization and rapid, accurate retrieval of numeric facts
examples: Encoding included 3 rounds of active-retrieval practice with feedback, a forced-choice test to determine if additional training was required, and a baseline test after a 30-minute break
key_sources: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9

article_title: Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood?
citation: L.M. Richter et al. (2021). Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood? npj Science of Learning 6:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00106-7
title: Nurturing Care Framework for early childhood environments
description: The Nurturing Care Framework (NCF), developed following the 2017 Lancet series on early childhood development, is a framework describing the qualities of environments that support young children's early learning and development. The article states it "describes the qualities of holistic environments that promote, support and protect young children 's health, nutrition, safety, and early learning, and satisfy the need for warm and affectionate responsiveness from others." It is used in the article to articulate why child-directed speech, emotional attunement and predictable adult responsiveness are foundations of children's learning from birth.
requirements: Environments must provide health, nutrition, safety and early learning supports together with warm and affectionate responsiveness from caregivers
target_learners: Young children from before birth through the preschool years
target_learning_goals: Early cognitive, language and socioemotional development; readiness for primary education
examples: The article cites the NCF as articulating the importance of child-directed speech, caregiver emotional attunement and predictable adult responsiveness as foundations of children's learning.
key_sources: L.M. Richter et al. (2021). Measuring and forecasting progress in education: what about early childhood? npj Science of Learning 6:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00106-7

article_title: Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood
citation: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1
title: Prioritise nurturing maths interest in adolescence to support STEM career pathways, over focusing only on reducing maths anxiety or raising self-efficacy
description: The article argues that because maths interest was the only construct that significantly and independently predicted actual STEM career choice for both sexes — remaining significant after adjusting for achievement and SES — educational effort should prioritise "enhancing maths interest in adolescence over merely reducing maths anxiety and increasing self-efficacy". It recommends developing targeted interventions fostering STEM participation aligned with the UK's need for STEM expertise.
requirements: Interventions target adolescence, when maths interest is measured and developing; effect sizes are modest (ORs 1.63–1.88).
constraints: The study design does not allow causal inference, so interventions rest on longitudinal associations, not tested causal effects.
target_learners: Adolescents (age ~16) in UK secondary education
target_learning_goals: Sustaining maths interest to support later STEM career participation
examples: The TEDS cohort study measured maths interest at age 16 with a three-item PISA-adapted scale (α = 0.93) and linked it to self-reported degree/apprenticeship choices at age ~21.
key_sources: Ferdinand, R., Malanchini, M. & Rimfeld, K. (2024). Mathematics interest, self-efficacy, and anxiety predict STEM career choice in emerging adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00275-1

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Nutritional label for Automated Decision Systems as the RDS course's object-to-interpret-with project deliverable
description: In the RDS course project, students design an original object-to-interpret-with in the form of a nutritional label for an Automated Decision System. "Adhering to constructivist principles, students develop nutritional labels for ADS." The label combines textual explanations and graphic information, requires students to distill the most important information about a model and adapt it for non-technical audiences, and functions as an end-to-end auditing device for the entire ADS.
requirements: Students are expected to have basic familiarity with the python programming language, which is used in labs and assignments.
constraints: The authors state the nutritional label is not the singular way to communicate a model to diverse audiences, since it does not make a model definitively interpretable to all stakeholders and for all purposes.
target_learners: graduate and advanced undergraduate data science students
target_learning_goals: making Automated Decision Systems interpretable
identifying intended audiences and non-transparent aspects of ADS
examples: The final course project combines elements of a replication study, process analysis, design and deployment, and nutritional label design; students replicate a model with an existing dataset and algorithm and identify transparency flaws.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Understanding students’ game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game
citation: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8
title: Number Navigation Game (NNG), an intrinsically integrated mathematics game for primary students
description: NNG is a mathematical game-based learning environment for primary school students focusing on flexibility and adaptivity with whole-number arithmetic. Players navigate a ship on a 100-square map by entering arithmetic operations to collect materials and return to harbor, with moves and energy scoring modes. The article describes it as having "an 'intrinsically integrated' design (Habgood and Ainsworth 2011a, b) in which the core gaming mechanism is integrated directly to the educational content of the game". It evolved through four versions from 2D simple graphics to a 3D Unity3D version with extrinsic motivational features.
requirements: Development demanded continuous testing and development activities, a multidisciplinary team of researchers, educators and programmers, and extensive research funding
constraints: The article notes intrinsically integrated games "can be more expensive and difficult to develop", and that funding limits hinder application of research-based games in the real world
target_learners: fourth to sixth grade primary school students
target_learning_goals: adaptive number knowledge
flexibility and adaptivity with whole-number arithmetic
maintaining interest in mathematics learning
examples: Across versions the game added a number pad, visual cues, pirate ships and hidden operations, a Shop, a Lighthouse Island, tutorial and hint options, and customization features
key_sources: Phuong Bui, Gabriela Rodríguez-Aflecht, Boglárka Brezovszky, Minna M. Hannula-Sormunen, Samuli Laato, Erno Lehtinen. (2020). Understanding students' game experiences throughout the developmental process of the number navigation game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09755-8

article_title: Nursery Rhyme Knowledge and Phonological Awareness in Preschool Children
citation: Harper, L. J. (2011). Nursery rhyme knowledge and phonological awareness in preschool children. The Journal of Language and Literacy Education [Online], 7(1), 65-78. https://jolle.coe.uga.edu
title: Nursery Rhyme Completion Statements assessment tool
description: A PowerPoint-format assessment composed of visual and auditory cues designed to assess children's existing knowledge of ten common nursery rhymes such as Humpty Dumpty and Itsy Bitsy Spider. Children were shown slides and asked if they knew who the pictures represented, with two prompts allowed, and were also asked where they learned the rhymes. Correct answers given to the initial statement or to either prompt earned one point.
requirements: Administered individually to children in the pre-K classroom context at the beginning and end of the study
constraints: The prompts for Humpty Dumpty are paraphrased rather than verbatim, which the author notes could confuse three-year-olds who learned the rhyme in its exact form
target_learners: three-year-old pre-K children
target_learning_goals: existing nursery rhyme knowledge
examples: Prompt #1 for Humpty Dumpty read '______________ sat on a wall and had a great fall'
key_sources: Harper, L. J. (2011). Nursery rhyme knowledge and phonological awareness in preschool children. The Journal of Language and Literacy Education [Online], 7(1), 65-78. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1097164

article_title: Nursery Rhyme Knowledge and Phonological Awareness in Preschool Children
citation: Harper, L. J. (2011). Nursery rhyme knowledge and phonological awareness in preschool children. The Journal of Language and Literacy Education [Online], 7(1), 65-78. https://jolle.coe.uga.edu
title: Integrating nursery rhymes and chants into the early childhood curriculum builds awareness of the sound patterns of language
description: The article argues that nursery rhymes are a socially engaging, playful, developmentally appropriate way for young children to hear, identify, manipulate, and experiment with the sounds of language. It states that "The use of nursery rhymes with young children promotes positive attitudes toward language learning and helps children to build awareness of sound patterns of language," and that combining tactile-kinesthetic activities within nursery rhyme contexts enhances phonological awareness and may stimulate phonemic skill development.
requirements: Children need many opportunities to use language in interactions with adults and to listen and respond to rhymes, chants and stories
constraints: The supporting study used only Euro-American nursery rhymes and a small sample
target_learners: preschool and pre-K children
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
phonemic sensitivity
early literacy development
examples: The ten-week intervention paired rhyme recitation with dramatization, prop boxes and felt-board retelling
key_sources: Harper, L. J. (2011). Nursery rhyme knowledge and phonological awareness in preschool children. The Journal of Language and Literacy Education [Online], 7(1), 65-78. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1097164

article_title: The Effects of Numbered Heads Together-Assurance Relevance Interest Assessment Satisfaction on Students' Motivation
citation: Mustami, M. K., & Safitri, D. (2018). The Effects of Numbered Heads Together -Assurance Relevance Interest Assessment Satisfaction on Students’ Motivation. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 123-134. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1139a
title: Numbered Heads Together cooperative learning model with group responsibility and prepared answering
description: NHT is a cooperative learning model in which students are divided into small groups and guided to do tasks together, emphasizing group work instead of individual work. The article describes it as "a variation of group discussion" in which all group members are responsible for the task, so each student must be prepared for the teacher's call to answer. It is presented as accommodating active participation across planning, implementation, and evaluation stages.
requirements: Small groups in which members share information and prepare together for the teacher's question call
constraints: The article reports it was studied only in senior high school biology classes, though the authors suggest elementary and junior high teachers can also implement it
target_learners: senior high school science students
low-ability students working alongside higher-ability peers
target_learning_goals: active participation
communication skills
learning motivation
examples: In the NHT-ARIAS classrooms, teachers appreciated students' work by giving rewards or compliments or claps to the best selected group, and low-ability students asked help from peers who mastered the subject better
key_sources: Mustami, M. K., & Safitri, D. (2018). The Effects of Numbered Heads Together -Assurance Relevance Interest Assessment Satisfaction on Students’ Motivation. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 123-134. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1139a

article_title: The Effectiveness of Teaching Number Relationships in Preschool
citation: Jung, M., Hartman, P., Smith, T., & Wallace, S. (2013). The Effectiveness of Teaching Number Relationships in Preschool. International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Number relationships framework: subitizing, parts-whole relationships, and more-and-less relationships
description: The article defines number relationships as "the ability to represent a quantity in multiple, flexible ways," going beyond counting skills. It organizes the construct into three features young children must develop: subitizing (instantly seeing a number without counting), parts-whole relationships (recognizing a whole can be partitioned into parts), and more-and-less relationships (understanding that the less quantity is contained in the more). The framework structures both the intervention activities and the study's hypothesis that increasing these skills increases mathematical understanding of number and quantity.
requirements: Instruction must give children experiences reflecting all key features of number relationships, which the authors say are connected and can be developed concurrently.
target_learners: preschool children ages 3 to 5
target_learning_goals: understanding of number and quantity
flexible representation of quantities
examples: Intervention teachers used rekenrek, Building Blocks software, and ten-frame activities so children could perceptually subitize counters, see more-and-less relations (1 less than 5), and view a whole made from sets of 2 and 2.
key_sources: Jung, M., Hartman, P., Smith, T., & Wallace, S. (2013). The Effectiveness of Teaching Number Relationships in Preschool. International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085361

article_title: From Efficacy Trial to Large Scale Effectiveness Trial: A Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention for First Graders with Difficulties in Mathematics
citation: Rolfhus, E., Gersten, R., Clarke, B., Decker, L., Wilkins, C., & Dimino, J. (2013). From Efficacy Trial to Large Scale Effectiveness Trial: A Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention for First Graders with Difficulties in Mathematics. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20124007/
title: Number Rockets Tier 2 small-group grade 1 mathematics intervention
description: Number Rockets is a supplemental small-group (two or three students) Tier 2 mathematics intervention for grade 1 students at risk for mathematics difficulties, meeting three or four times weekly from November to May. It "covers 17 topics, each divided into three to six lessons, not all of which are required," with mastery-based skipping of extra lessons; students averaged 45 lessons of about 40 minutes delivered by part-time interventionists using scripted lessons during regular school hours.
requirements: Delivered by interventionists following a lesson script with prescribed feedback and prompting procedures
Used strictly as a supplemental mathematics program per developer instructions
constraints: In this study delivered as pullout sessions during regular school hours, with the last 10 minutes devoted to individualized addition/subtraction flashcard practice
target_learners: Grade 1 students at risk for mathematics difficulties (lowest 35 percent on a screening composite)
target_learning_goals: Early mathematics achievement (formal and informal mathematics skills measured by TEMA-3)
examples: In the effectiveness trial, 86 locally recruited interventionists with a wide range of teaching experience delivered the program after one 8-hour training and two 2-hour follow-up trainings, with questions answered via email or telephone
key_sources: Rolfhus, E., Gersten, R., Clarke, B., Decker, L., Wilkins, C., & Dimino, J. (2013). From Efficacy Trial to Large Scale Effectiveness Trial: A Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention for First Graders with Difficulties in Mathematics. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20124007/

article_title: From Efficacy Trial to Large Scale Effectiveness Trial: A Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention for First Graders with Difficulties in Mathematics
citation: Rolfhus, E., Gersten, R., Clarke, B., Decker, L., Wilkins, C., & Dimino, J. (2013). From Efficacy Trial to Large Scale Effectiveness Trial: A Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention for First Graders with Difficulties in Mathematics. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20124007/
title: Scripted small-group Tier 2 intervention with mastery-based topic progression, individualized fact practice, and a points-based behavior management system
description: The intervention combines several recurring design features: highly prescribed scripted lessons with specified feedback and prompting; mastery criteria that allow skipping additional lessons once the whole group meets criteria; individualized flashcard fact practice whose "difficulty of the flashcards increased with the skill of individual student"; and a positive-reinforcement behavior system awarding points for accomplishment, mastery, and randomly timed engagement checks, with small rewards roughly every two sessions.
requirements: Interventionists able to follow a prescribed lesson script and prepare individualized flashcard decks before each lesson
A screening procedure to identify at-risk students before assignment to groups
constraints: Fact practice difficulty is independent of the group's progression through the lessons
target_learners: Grade 1 students at risk for mathematics difficulties in Tier 2 RtI settings
target_learning_goals: Early mathematics proficiency and addition/subtraction fact fluency
examples: Sessions ran about 40 minutes, typically three or four times per week from November to May, with most students earning a reward approximately every two sessions

article_title: The Practices of Critical Thinking Component and Its Impact in Malaysian Nurses Health Education
citation: Abdul Ghani Kanesan Abdullah, Naser Jamil Alzaidiyeen, Ng Mooi Yee. (2010). The Practices of Critical Thinking Component and Its Impact in Malaysian Nurses Health Education. International Education Studies, 3(1). https://journals.ccsenet.org/index.php/ies
title: Nurse teachers should themselves be knowledgeable practitioners of critical thinking and provide explicit guidance and feedback
description: In its implications, the article argues that nurse trainers should be knowledgeable and practitioners of critical thinking, because understanding the theory of critical thinking gives the teacher a better perception of an argument and "a foundatio n for explicit guidance and feedback on her stude nts". It further states that the key to mastering the skill of critical thinking is constant deliberate practice, so teachers who handle arguments often reinforce their own beliefs in critical thinking and model it for future nurses.
requirements: Nurse teachers must understand critical thinking theory and practice it themselves to guide and give feedback to students
constraints: The article frames this as an implication of the study rather than a tested manipulation
target_learners: student nurses and their nurse teachers
target_learning_goals: critical thinking capability for effective health education delivery
examples: The article recommends nurse teachers use their expert, resource and position power to influence students, grounded in the finding that thinking skills need to be nurtured rather than appearing suddenly

article_title: An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes
citation: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229
title: NumberShire Level 1 game-based Tier 2 mathematics intervention
description: NS1 is a game-based, Tier 2 mathematics intervention for first-grade students with or at risk for mathematics difficulties, integrating explicit instruction, whole-number content, and an engaging gaming platform set in a Renaissance-style fairy tale village. "NS1 consists of 48 sessions, themed into 12 weeks of instruction (four sessions per week). Each session is designed to provide 15 minutes of instruction." Sessions comprise Warm-Up, Teaching Event, Assessment Event, and Wrap-Up activities with virtual representations, frequent practice opportunities, and academic feedback.
requirements: Delivered in school computer labs by trained interventionists who monitor gameplay but provide no instructional assistance during sessions
Four hours of professional development covering group facilitation, technical troubleshooting, and progress monitoring
constraints: The study tested only an abbreviated version: 8 weeks of the full 12-week intervention, due to a final round of revisions and SBIR funding
target_learners: first-grade students with or at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: whole-number concepts and skills: counting and cardinality, number and operations in base ten, operations and algebraic thinking
examples: In the pilot RCT, treatment students averaged 18.6 game sessions and 499.8 practice opportunities at 69% accuracy over eight weeks
key_sources: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229

article_title: The Cognitive Processing Potential of Infants: Exploring the Impact of an Early Childhood Development Programme
citation: van Eeden, R. & van Vuuren, J., 2017, 'The cognitive processing potential of infants: Exploring the impact of an early childhood development programme', South African Journal of Childhood Education 7(1), a499. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajce.v7i1.499
title: Numbers in Nappies programme
description: A parent-delivered early childhood development programme developed for this study, using flashcards of numbers, shapes and colours shown to infants for approximately 2–3 seconds each. The article states the programme "is applied on a daily basis, two to three times a day, for approximately 1 min per session, over an average of 60 days", with stimuli presented visually via flashcards and auditorily through the parent's voice. It avoids technology and promotes bonding in a positive learning environment.
requirements: Parent or primary caregiver delivery through direct daily communication, with training provided to parents before implementation
constraints: Developed as part of the present study and therefore not previously evaluated; evaluated only in a middle-income-sector sample of infants without developmental problems
target_learners: infants aged 3–12 months
target_learning_goals: number concepts including addition, subtraction, multiplication, greater than and less than
shape and colour recognition
memory, problem solving, classification and attention maintenance
examples: In the study, parents of the intervention group were trained in the programme and implemented it daily for approximately two months, with nine mothers also participating in fortnightly discussions to monitor participation
key_sources: van Eeden, R. & van Vuuren, J., 2017, 'The cognitive processing potential of infants: Exploring the impact of an early childhood development programme', South African Journal of Childhood Education 7(1), a499. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajce.v7i1.499

article_title: Development of an Instructional Quality Assurance Model in Nursing Science
citation: Haruthai Ajpru, Shotiga Pasiphol, Suwimon Wongwanich. (2008). Development of an instructional quality assurance model in nursing science. Research in Higher Education Journal. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: A systematic instructional quality assurance model for nursing science consisting of input, process and output across principles, concepts and practice
description: The developed model is a systematic instructional quality assurance model for nursing science. As the article states, "The instructional quality assurance model in nursing science was systematic consisting of input, process and output. The operation was based on 3 domains: principles, concepts and practice." It comprises 6 standards and 18 indicators, with the curriculum standard holding 3 indicators, instructional support 4, nursing instructor 2, instruction 4, learning evaluation and assessment 3, and nursing student/graduate 2, plus 21 elements of guidelines. It aligns with ONESQA standards 1, 5 and 6, Nursing Council instructional elements and the Thailand Qualification Framework.
requirements: Developed for academic divisions of nursing educational institutions responsible for curriculum administration and lesson plan
constraints: Indicators were kept few, per the principle that "there should not be too many indicators"; institutions may adapt the 11 general rules for appropriateness in their own institution
target_learners: nursing science students in Thai higher education
target_learning_goals: instructional quality assurance in nursing science programs
examples: Audit and evaluation by meta-evaluation rated the model good overall (X = 4.32), with usefulness and innovative aspect very good (X = 4.75 and 4.62)
key_sources: Haruthai Ajpru, Shotiga Pasiphol, Suwimon Wongwanich. (2008). Development of an instructional quality assurance model in nursing science. Research in Higher Education Journal. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ

article_title: Application of the modified Mini-CEX combined with the SBAR model in the experimental teaching of health assessment course: a quasi-experimental study.

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10086-0
title: Standardized patient program using trained nursing students as simulated patients
description: The study used standardized patients to create strong clinical situations: "SPs selected included 30 undergraduate nursing students who were taking Health Assessment course from the class of 2020." After systematic training, these 30 students "could accurately demonstrate the corresponding clinical symptoms and some signs of patients with related diseases." Four backbone teachers obtained SP trainer certification to run the program.
requirements: SP trainer certification and systematic SP training according to training requirements
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: clinical simulation participation
history taking and physical examination practice

article_title: Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial.
citation: Ivo Bril-Broers, Nick Degens, Joke Fleer. (2026). Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/91083
title: Self-regulated learning cycle model underlying the Nurse-IT reflection app
description: The app was designed around "a self-regulated learning cycle which starts at the forethought phase, to then monitor oneself in the performance phase, and to evaluate oneself in the self-reflection phase after which the cycle begins anew." Learning goals and tasks instantiate the forethought phase, daily reflections the performance phase, and weekly reflections the self-reflection phase, combined with experiential learning and persuasive systems design principles.
requirements: Consistent student use, since "an educational app is dependent on students using it consistently"
constraints: The study found students can go through SRL phases outside the app and that self-regulated learning is not a strictly linear process
target_learners: nursing students on clinical placement
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
socioemotional competence development
examples: The app's home screen shows learning goals with tasks; the learning goal overview visualizes daily reflection grades over time (1-3 red, 4-6 yellow, 7-10 green)
key_sources: Ivo Bril-Broers, Nick Degens, Joke Fleer. (2026). Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/91083

article_title: Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice.
citation: Aldawood Fatima Dawood, Shamas Nour, Alshamrani Majid. (2026). Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09314-4
title: A 12-topic nursing antimicrobial stewardship course curriculum
description: The developed curriculum comprises 12 topics delivered in a nursing AMS course: AMS and nurses' role; basic microbiology; basic pharmacology and antibiotic classes; AMS strategies and policies; nurses' role in improving antimicrobial allergy labelling; infection prevention and control; optimal microbiology testing and drug level sampling; safe antimicrobial storage and administration; AMS in sepsis; AMS clinical pearls; patient education; and nursing empowerment in AMS. Topics were "intentionally arranged such that the course starts with foundational concepts" with topics requiring greater clinical judgment placed later to build knowledge and enable informed clinical reasoning.
requirements: A lesson plan structured into eight components including topics, learning objectives, content outline, teaching strategies, educational materials, formative evaluation methods, modifications, and estimated delivery time
constraints: The curriculum was developed considering the scope of practice of the hospital's nurses and to meet the institution's needs, which may limit generalizability to different settings
target_learners: Registered nurses at a tertiary healthcare institution
target_learning_goals: Antimicrobial stewardship knowledge, clinical practice, and patient education skills
examples: A detailed lesson plan for topic 5 on nurses' role in improving antimicrobial allergy labelling includes case scenarios, didactic lecture, discussion, and reflection over 30 minutes
key_sources: Aldawood Fatima Dawood, Shamas Nour, Alshamrani Majid. (2026). Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09314-4

article_title: Perspectives and challenges in implementing nursing-specific mini-CEX and DOPS: a descriptive qualitative study of clinical nursing educators and novice nurses in a tertiary hospital in China.
citation: Nie Shengxiao, Ma Shengmiao, Wang Lei. (2026). Perspectives and challenges in implementing nursing-specific mini-CEX and DOPS: a descriptive qualitative study of clinical nursing educators and novice nurses in a tertiary hospital in China. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-113912
title: Nursing-specific mini-CEX and DOPS assessment forms
description: The revised mini-CEX includes seven dimensions (patient interviews, physical examinations, empathy, professionalism, clinical judgement, counselling, overall efficiency) scored on a 9-point scale via bedside observation; the revised DOPS form includes eight aspects (knowledge, patient consent, technical competence, smooth techniques, seeking assistance, communication, humanitarianism, overall performance) on a 0–5 scale. "Both mini-CEX and DOPS forms include self-evaluation and evaluator comments as open questions."
requirements: Educator training before implementation to ensure mastery of usage, evaluation frequency and form norms
constraints: Forms are universal and lack department-specific specialty
target_learners: novice nurses
target_learning_goals: clinical skills assessment and formative feedback
examples: During months 1–6, novice nurses complete ≥1 mini-CEX per 2 months and ≥2 DOPS per month; months 7–12 require ≥1 of each per month
key_sources: Nie Shengxiao, Ma Shengmiao, Wang Lei. (2026). article_title: Expert Consensus on Key Attributes of Nurses in Resuscitation Teams: Findings From a Delphi Study.
citation: Kipourgos George, Bakalis Nick, Albani Eleni, Stefanopoulos Nikolaos, Lakoumentas John, Tzenalis Anastasios. (2026). Expert Consensus on Key Attributes of Nurses in Resuscitation Teams: Findings From a Delphi Study. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70506
title: Seven-domain expert-validated framework of nursing attributes for in-hospital resuscitation teams
description: A consensus-based framework of 35 validated attributes characterizing effective nursing participation in in-hospital cardiac arrest teams, generated through a two-round partially electronic Delphi with 15 experts. Thematic analysis of round-one interviews produced "a total of 39 distinct attributes... categorized into seven thematic domains": education, age, experience, physical condition, mental condition, technical skills and non-technical skills. Round-two rating retained 35 attributes, with strongest consensus in the non-technical and technical skills domains. The authors position it as "a consensus-based conceptual foundation rather than a ready-to-use assessment or selection tool" for curricula, competency development and team composition.
requirements: Further psychometric validation before operationalization into standardized measurement instruments or formal performance appraisal
constraints: Based solely on subjective expert judgements without correlation to objective performance indicators such as ROSC, response time or survival to discharge
All experts were recruited from Greece, so national training pathways and team organization may limit transferability to other healthcare systems
target_learners: Nurses participating in in-hospital resuscitation teams
Nursing students and trainees in critical care and emergency settings
target_learning_goals: Resuscitation technical competencies
Non-technical skills including communication, teamwork, leadership and resilience
examples: Round one used semi-structured interviews with 15 experts analysed thematically; round two rated 39 statements on a 10-point Likert scale via the Typeform platform with a 100% response rate
key_sources: Kipourgos George, Bakalis Nick, Albani Eleni, Stefanopoulos Nikolaos, Lakoumentas John, Tzenalis Anastasios. (2026). Expert Consensus on Key Attributes of Nurses in Resuscitation Teams: Findings From a Delphi Study. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70506

article_title: UAB/SNMMI Nuclear Medicine Therapy Intensive: Advancing Competence and Innovation in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
citation: Glasgow KW, Brady AB. (2025). UAB/SNMMI Nuclear Medicine Therapy Intensive: Advancing Competence and Innovation in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology. https://doi.org/10.2967/jnmt.125.271222
title: Nuclear medicine therapy escape room: a team-based, case-puzzle capstone applying clinical reasoning, dose calculation, and safety decision-making
description: The nuclear medicine therapy escape room is the program's capstone event, described by the authors as "a first-of-its-kind capstone event in the field of nuclear medicine therapy". Teams solve case-based puzzles requiring "clinical reasoning, dose calculation, radiopharmaceutical selection, and workflow problem-solving" under time pressure in a team-based format. The authors cite reviews and meta-analyses finding educational escape rooms improve cognitive, psychomotor, affective, and nontechnical skills, and report it received the program's strongest satisfaction ratings.
requirements: Case-based puzzles integrating dose calculation, radiopharmaceutical selection, workflow problem-solving, and safety decision-making
Timed, team-based format
Placement as a capstone after didactic and simulation components
target_learners: Practicing nuclear medicine technologists and advanced associates in the intensive
target_learning_goals: Applying therapy knowledge to clinical reasoning and workflow decision-making under time pressure
Teamwork on case-based therapy scenarios
examples: Participants collaborated in the escape room as shown in Figure 7, applying clinical reasoning, radiopharmaceutical selection, and workflow problem-solving
key_sources: Glasgow KW, Brady AB. (2025). UAB/SNMMI Nuclear Medicine Therapy Intensive: Advancing Competence and Innovation in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology. https://doi.org/10.2967/jnmt.125.271222

article_title: Teachers' Strategies and Technology Use for Enhancing Students' Critical Thinking in Nursing Simulation-Based Learning: A Qualitative Pilot Study.
citation: Malin Forsbrand, Line Christiansen, Vicky Johnson Gatzouras. (2025). Teachers’ Strategies and Technology Use for Enhancing Students’ Critical Thinking in Nursing Simulation-Based Learning: A Qualitative Pilot Study. Inquiry: A Journal of Medical Care Organization, Provision and Financing. https://doi.org/10.1177/00469580251392452
title: Simulation technology set used in nursing SBL: high-fidelity mannequins, tablets, microphones, cameras, large screens, and communication platforms such as Zoom
description: The pilot describes the concrete technologies teachers used to support nursing students' CT in SBL. "The participants used high-fidelity mannequins (e.g., a digitally connected simulation doll) and more common technologies (e.g., tablet device, microphones, cameras and large screens) to monitor, communicate and modify simulations." Communication platforms such as Zoom were used to simulate scenarios and train students in distance health dialogue with patients, and technologies allowed teachers to remotely control and adjust the mannequin's functions.
requirements: Practical preparation including functional tests of the technical equipment configured to the specific patient case for each scenario
constraints: The technology-related findings depend on universities' access to simulation technologies, so conditions differ between universities
target_learners: nursing students in higher education
target_learning_goals: applying theoretical knowledge in realistic clinical scenarios and developing critical thinking
examples: A high-fidelity mannequin served as a fictive patient whose vital signs students monitored via a tablet, while microphones inside the control and simulation rooms facilitated communication

Teachers’ Strategies and Technology Use for Enhancing Students’ Critical Thinking in Nursing Simulation-Based Learning: A Qualitative Pilot Study. article_title: Explaining reasons for cheating in exams among undergraduate nursing students: a qualitative study.
citation: Mousavi SK, Kamali M. (2025). Explaining reasons for cheating in exams among undergraduate nursing students: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07693-8
title: Two-theme taxonomy of reasons for exam cheating among nursing students: personal and organizational factors
description: The article develops an inductive qualitative taxonomy of the reasons undergraduate nursing students cheat on exams. From interviews with 15 participants, 189 initial codes were reduced to 96 final codes organized into 14 subcategories, four categories, and two themes. As the authors state, "the reasons for academic cheating in nursing students included two groups of personal and organizational factors", with personal factors split into intrapersonal and interpersonal categories and organizational factors into policy weaknesses and implementation problems.
requirements: Purposeful sampling of information-rich participants including students with a history of cheating and faculty/administrators
constraints: Findings derive from two nursing colleges affiliated with Zanjan University of Medical Sciences, Iran
The authors note the study lacked detailed discussion of the extracted themes given the complexity of the phenomenon
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: understanding and preventing academic cheating in examinations
examples: Semi-structured interviews of 30 to 60 minutes were analyzed with Elo and Kyngas' inductive content analysis using MAXQDA 2020, with saturation reached after 14 interviews
key_sources: Mousavi SK, Kamali M. (2025). Explaining reasons for cheating in exams among undergraduate nursing students: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07693-8

article_title: The competency of nurses in basic life support at district hospitals in Cape Town, South Africa.
citation: Mahembe GR, Mash R. (2025). The competency of nurses in basic life support at district hospitals in Cape Town, South Africa. S Afr Fam Pract. https://doi.org/10.4102/safp.v67i1.6056
title: Maintain a staffing mix weighted towards more-qualified nurses to support BLS competency and clinical mentoring
description: The article argues that the ratio of more to less qualified nurses matters for BLS competency: the observed EN:PN:PNS ratio of 1:0.9:0.4 fell far below the recommended 1:1:1 norm. It recommends attention to the workforce mix because "more highly trained and qualified nurses can also provide clinical mentoring to more junior colleagues", and cites evidence that facilities with more bachelor's-degree nurses have lower mortality and better resuscitation outcomes.
requirements: A workforce containing enough professional and bachelor's-degree nurses to mentor junior colleagues
constraints: More advanced qualifications and ranks made up a small proportion of the study workforce
target_learners: Nurses in district hospitals, particularly enrolled nurses and nursing assistants
target_learning_goals: Basic life support competency
Clinical mentoring of junior nursing staff
examples: The study measured an EN:PN:PNS ratio of 1:0.9:0.4 against the recommended 1:1:1 staffing norm
key_sources: Mahembe GR, Mash R. (2025). The competency of nurses in basic life support at district hospitals in Cape Town, South Africa. S Afr Fam Pract. https://doi.org/10.4102/safp.v67i1.6056

article_title: Performance of ChatGPT on Nursing Licensure Examinations in the United States and China: Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Wu Zelin, Gan Wenyi, Xue Zhaowen, Ni Zhengxin, Zheng Xiaofei, Zhang Yiyi. (2024). Performance of ChatGPT on Nursing Licensure Examinations in the United States and China: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/52746

description: A compiled dataset of 618 nursing multiple-choice questions used to evaluate LLM performance: 150 NCLEX-RN practice MCQs from nurseslabs and 468 NNLE actual exam questions (2021-2022) from Baidu, split into theoretical and practical sections, with image questions excluded. Questions were translated between English and Chinese using ChatGPT 3.5, and the full dataset was "recorded in an Excel file and uploaded as Multimedia Appendix 1."

constraints: Image-based questions were excluded because ChatGPT and Google Bard picture analysis required external plug-ins
target_learners: nursing students
nursing licensure candidates
target_learning_goals: assessing LLM performance on nursing theoretical and practical knowledge questions
examples: 150 NCLEX-RN practical MCQs, 235 NNLE theoretical MCQs, and 233 NNLE practical MCQs were input into three LLMs in two languages

article_title: Perceptions of medical students at Najran University on the effectiveness of problem-based learning and team-based learning.
citation: Almagribi Ahmad Zaker, Al-Qahtani Saad Misfer, Assiri Abdullah M., Mehdar Khlood Mohammed. (2024). Perceptions of medical students at Najran University on the effectiveness of problem-based learning and team-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06148-w
title: PBL seven jumps approach and TBL five steps as implemented at Najran University
description: The article documents two locally implemented structured protocols for the student-centered approaches it surveys. "The PBL is applied using the seven jumps approach as illustrated in Fig. 1" and "The TBL is applied employing the five steps as shown in Fig. 2"; TBL is described in the introduction as "a highly structured approach involving students and requires particular steps and core elements for implementation", applicable to both large and small classes. These figures operationalise the two models whose perceptions the survey measures.
requirements: TBL implementation requires particular steps and core elements and lecturer involvement as students reported
constraints: The PBL and TBL protocols described are those applied in the preclinical phases of the NU medical program specifically
target_learners: preclinical medical students (years 2-4) at Najran University
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
teamwork and communication skills
motivation to study
examples: NU applies PBL via the seven jumps approach (Fig. 1) and TBL via five steps (Fig. 2) within horizontally and vertically integrated preclinical blocks
key_sources: Almagribi Ahmad Zaker, Al-Qahtani Saad Misfer, Assiri Abdullah M., Mehdar Khlood Mohammed. (2024).
